splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This split produces dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on where they are prosecuted.

positions.label: Conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria are met.

positions.label: Disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' should be read disjunctively or distributively, so possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal statutes or sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should prevail over deference to an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous provision in a criminal or sentencing context. The Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails. This split affects how criminal defendants are sentenced under ambiguous guideline provisions.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous guidelines enhancements in criminal cases.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2) can authoritatively expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1, which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation of the guideline entitled to deference under Stinson, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary cannot expand the definition beyond the text, so conspiracy convictions do not qualify as controlled substance offenses.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state controls a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled, or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects base offense levels and career-offender determinations for defendants with prior state drug convictions for substances not scheduled under federal law.

positions.label: State-scheduled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that to qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines, the substance must be controlled under federal law, not merely under state law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) authorizing such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law—particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked 25-year minimums for § 924(c) convictions—as grounds for compassionate release. Some circuits allow it while others hold it is categorically barred. The Seventh Circuit has held the Commission's 2024 policy statement purporting to authorize it exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, may be considered alone or in combination with other factors as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement saying otherwise exceeds its statutory authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the terms (but not necessarily the fact or duration) of imprisonment must proceed under habeas corpus or may bring claims under civil rights statutes (e.g., Bivens or § 2241).
splits.description: Since Preiser v. Rodriguez, circuits have been deeply divided on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges that touch on confinement conditions or BOP transfer/custody decisions, or whether prisoners may also use civil rights actions. This longstanding split affects the procedural avenues available to federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions, including First Step Act time-credit calculations.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges affecting confinement duration
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration or execution of a sentence, including First Step Act time credits, must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are also available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights actions (not just habeas) to challenge conditions of confinement or certain BOP decisions that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose sentences at supervised release revocation to punish defendants for their violations, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to addressing the breach of trust and protecting the public.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that the purpose of revocation sentencing is to address the breach of trust in the supervisory relationship, not to punish for the underlying violation conduct. This split affects how hundreds of revocation sentences are imposed each year.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permitted
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants at revocation for their supervised release violations, following United States v. Lewis.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must address breach of trust, not punish
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of a revocation sentence is to sanction the breach of trust inherent in the violation of supervised release conditions, not to punish the defendant for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that accrues between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or belongs to the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate, while other circuits have reached the opposite conclusion. This split affects debtors who convert in good faith and may lose significant home equity.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion, consistent with the statute's structure and legislative history.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil appeal timeline (30 days under FRAP 4(a)) or the criminal appeal timeline (14 days under FRAP 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, filed in a criminal case, is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the appellate deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fees motion is ancillary to the criminal case, but a minority of circuits apply the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under FRAP 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fees order arises in a criminal case and is governed by the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under FRAP 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing rules for actuarial assumption selection in calculating employer withdrawal liability under ERISA's multiemployer pension provisions. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing of when actuarial assumptions can be selected directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by the measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be determined as of the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year) and cannot be selected after that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after the measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select assumptions after the measurement date, as long as the assumptions are applied to data as of that date, giving plans flexibility in their calculations.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: GCIU-Employer Retirement Fund v. Goldfarb Corp.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises fundamental questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, so the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, so the term expires as specified in the judgment regardless of flight.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Six circuits hold that § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring claims that were previously presented, while three circuits hold it does not apply and that federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate gatekeeping requirements. This 6-to-3 split creates disparate treatment of federal prisoners seeking to challenge their convictions based on the circuit in which they were convicted.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously presented claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of new evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures like mail-in ballot deadlines. If standing is broadly granted, it would make it far easier to challenge election rules nationwide; if denied, such disputes would be deferred until post-election, creating significant practical complications.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge election administration rules before an election, based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful vote-counting procedures.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge state election procedures pre-election because competitive injury from ballot-counting rules is too speculative.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine of 28 U.S.C. § 1291.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable as collateral orders because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost without immediate review. Other circuits have applied the collateral order doctrine more restrictively to sealing motions, creating tension on when privacy-related sealing denials qualify for interlocutory appeal.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated on post-judgment appeal.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the right can be adequately vindicated through other means, including protective orders or post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have developed differing approaches to discrimination claims in hospitality and business settings, including standards for liability and available remedies. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a split involving the Second Circuit's approach to these questions, which could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit's approach
positions.summary: Applied a standard for discrimination claims in hospitality settings that the Supreme Court found sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting the approach may differ from other circuits.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different or more established standards for evaluating discrimination and fair treatment claims against business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
